Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting

Baochun Li University of Toronto

Zongpeng Li Tsinghua University

Sirui Liu Tsinghua University

**Abstract**

Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages. Fractional routing instead splits each message among source--destination paths and forwards its parts without combining different messages. For undirected networks carrying independent messages between multiple source-- destination pairs, the multiple-unicast conjecture asserts that the two methods achieve the same combinations of message rates. We give a finite counterexample and use its linear structure to accelerate external-memory integer sorting, addressing the question of whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound posed by Aggarwal and Vitter in 1988.

We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for _N_ integers of \(\Theta(logN)\) bits, a memory holding _M_ integers, and block transfers of _B_ integers, where \(2B\le M\le N\), the number of block transfers is

\(O\big(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{logN}{(log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(logM)^\varepsilon}\right]\big),\)

where \(\varepsilon=1.5\times 10^{-5}\) is an absolute constant. In some parameter ranges, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm’s correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean.

## 1 Introduction

A multiple-unicast network carries independent messages between specified source-destination pairs. Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages. Fractional routing instead splits each message among paths and forwards the resulting parts without mixing messages. In 2004, Li and Li proposed the multiple-unicast conjecture: network coding and fractional routing achieve the same message rates in undirected multiple-unicast networks \[LL04\]. The conjecture is also closely connected to several important problems in theoretical computer science; if true, it would imply conditional complexity lower bounds, including for external-memory integer sorting \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>06, FHLS19,AFKL19\].

In 2026, Zhang, Li, and Li \[ZLL26\] and Braverman and He \[BH26\] constructed counterexamples in undirected multiple-unicast networks, showing that network coding can strictly outperform fractional routing and thereby refuting the multiple-unicast conjecture. These counterexamples establish a communication advantage, but invalidating the assumption behind a conditional lower bound does not itself produce a faster algorithm.

External-memory integer sorting is one problem closely tied to the conjecture. The _N_ input integers are stored on disk, with one integer per machine word, a fixed-size unit of storage. Memory holds _M_ words, and each transfer between disk and memory moves one block of _B_ consecutive words. The input/output (I/O) complexity is the total number of these transfers. The optimal classical comparison-sorting bound is \[AV88\]

\(\Theta\big(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{log(N/M)}{log(M/B)}\right]\big).\) (1)

In 1988, Aggarwal and Vitter asked whether allowing algorithms to exploit the bits of integer keys could improve on this comparison bound \[AV88\]. This has long been a central open problem in external-memory algorithms \[FHLS19\]. Farhadi, Hajiaghayi, Larsen, and Shi \[FHLS19\] proved that, if the multiple-unicast conjecture were true, then for \(B\ge logN\), integer sorting could not asymptotically improve on the comparison-sorting I/O bound, even with arbitrary bit operations.

We turn the communication advantage of coding into fewer block transfers. We first construct a finite undirected multiple-unicast network in which binary linear coding strictly outperforms fractional routing. We use the finite circuit to interchange two address fields, meaning two groups of consecutive digits in an array position. Recursive calls interchange progressively shorter fields; once enough buffers fit in memory, scans perform the remaining movement directly. Building on existing recursive field-exchange techniques \[Ope26\], we combine this operation with Columnsort, which alternates sorting columns with fixed rearrangements, and most-significant-digit (MSD) radix sorting, which partitions integers by their high-order bits first.

Specifically, for every \(2B\le M\le N\), our algorithm sorts _N_ integers of \(\Theta(logN)\) bits in

\(O\big(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{logN}{(log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(logM)^\varepsilon}\right]\big)\)

I/Os, where the absolute constant can be taken as \(\varepsilon=1.5\times 10^{-5}>0\). The algorithm is correct for every input, including repeated values, and uses at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space under the conventions of Section 3. When \(w<\lceil log_2N\rceil\) and _M_ is below a fixed threshold, those conventions allow the predetermined execution-step index to be stored outside the _M_ words. In particular, when _M_=2_B_ and _N=B_<sup>2</sup>, classical comparison sorting requires \(\Theta(BlogB)\) I/Os, whereas our algorithm uses \(O(B(logB)^{1-\varepsilon})\).

### Formal verification.

Using Lean 4 \[dU21\], we have formally verified the sorting algorithm’s correctness and I/O complexity bound under the model of Section 3.<sup>1</sup> The verification covers \(\varepsilon=1.5\times 10^{-5}\) and all parameter ranges of Theorem 3.1. Appendix D gives the formal statements and verification details.

Section 2 reviews related work. Sections 3-4 give the model, main results, and proof overview. Section 5 constructs the coding counterexample, and Section 6 applies it to address-field interchange. Sections 7-8 construct the sorting algorithm and complete the main proof. The appendices supply memory simulation, fixed-parameter calculations, interchange for general field widths and prefix counts, and formalization details.

## 2 Related work

### External-memory sorting.

Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) \[AV88\] established the classical I/O bounds for sorting and related problems, with multiway merge sort and distribution sort attaining the optimal comparison-sorting complexity. Their separate lower bound under record indivisibility also explains the cost of rearranging records, while leaving open what can be achieved by encoding their bits. The subsequent development of external-memory algorithms is surveyed by Vitter (2001) \[Vit01\]. Frigo, Leiserson, Prokop, and Ramachandran (1999) \[FLPR99\] introduced cache- oblivious sorting algorithms that attain optimal comparison I/O complexity without knowing _M_ or _B_, under the tall-cache assumption \(M=\Omega(B^2)\). Arge and Thorup \[AT15\] later combined external distribution sorting with integer-sorting techniques to improve internal computation time while retaining the classical comparison-sorting I/O bound.

Integer representations have nevertheless yielded I/O improvements for other external-memory problems. Iacono and Pˇatraşcu (2012) \[IP12\] used hashing to improve dictionary updates beyond comparison-based bounds and proved a matching lower bound in the external-memory cell-probe model, which charges for accessing stored blocks rather than for computation. Jiang and Larsen (2019) \[JL19\] obtained faster external-memory priority queues supporting DecreaseKey, the operation that lowers an existing item’s priority. These results concern different operations and do not themselves improve the I/O bound for general sorting. For general integer sorting, Farhadi, Hajiaghayi, Larsen, and Shi (2019) \[FHLS19\] proved an I/O lower bound conditional on the multiple- unicast conjecture, even allowing arbitrary bit operations. Since the conjecture has been refuted, this implication does not establish an unconditional sorting lower bound.

Our sorting construction uses a different established line of work. Leighton’s (1985) Columnsort \[Lei85\] alternates column sorts with fixed permutations. Chaudhry, Cormen, and Wisniewski (2001) \[CCW01\] developed an external-memory implementation, and Chaudhry and Cormen (2006) \[CC06\] developed Slabpose Columnsort to relax problem-size restrictions for distributed-memory clusters. Our algorithm uses classical Columnsort and accelerates its fixed permutations. The rearrangement method builds on OpenAI’s (2026) integer-multiplication work \[Ope26\], which recursively exploits finite linear-circuit savings to accelerate address-field interchange on a multitape Turing machine. We adapt this method to block transfers through memory-dependent recursion base cases, buffering, padding, and space bounds, then combine it with Columnsort and most-significant-digit radix partitioning.

### The multiple-unicast conjecture.

Li and Li (2004) \[LL04\] conjectured that network coding cannot improve the achievable rates of independent multiple-unicast sessions over fractional routing in undirected networks. Subsequent work proved the conjecture in special cases with restrictions on network structure and terminal placement \[JVY06,HKL06,YLLW18,QT22\], and developed geometric and metric approaches \[XLWH14,LL25,LQLL26\] and frameworks based on relations among sessions \[LHWL26,LLFC26\]. Related routing results characterize when cut conditions suffice for multiflow in series-parallel networks \[CFW12\]. The conjecture also became closely connected to computational lower bounds. Adler, Harvey, Jain, Kleinberg, and Lehman (2006) \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>06\] first used it to prove conditional lower bounds in several computational models whose access patterns are independent of the input. Farhadi, Hajiaghayi, Larsen, and Shi (2019) \[FHLS19\] removed this access restriction for external-memory integer sorting: assuming the conjecture, any randomized sorting algorithm with error probability at most 1/3 and key length \(w=\Omega(logN)\) requires at least

\(\Omega\left(min\big\{N,\frac{N}{B}log_{2M/B}\frac{N}{B}\big\}\right)\)

expected I/Os. Under the same assumption, when \(B\ge logN\), this lower bound would match the classical comparison-sorting bound up to constant factors. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma, and Larsen (2019) \[AFKL19\] extended this connection to integer multiplication, obtaining conditional lower bounds for constant-degree Boolean circuits and further demonstrating the conjecture’s complexity- theoretic significance beyond communication problems.

The finite binary linear circuit in OpenAI’s integer-multiplication construction \[Ope26, Section 3\] also implies a counterexample to the multiple-unicast conjecture. This follows by applying the routing argument in Section 5.4 to its rational matrix labels, which gives a routing upper bound strictly below an achievable coding rate.

Recently, Zhang, Li, and Li (2026) \[ZLL26\] and Braverman and He (2026) \[BH26\] gave counterexamples to the multiple-unicast conjecture, proving that coding can achieve strictly higher throughput than fractional routing. The former construct a reversible communication process from a completion-time separation; the latter use finite geometry and polynomial evaluation to construct a coding scheme. These results establish the existence of a coding advantage, but refuting the conjecture does not by itself produce a faster sorting algorithm. We further study how such an advantage can reduce data movement in computation: the finite linear construction used here both yields a communication-rate separation and supports recursive address permutations, connecting network-coding constructions to I/O upper bounds for external-memory sorting.

## 3 Main Results

We write log for the base-2 logarithm and ln for the natural logarithm. For a positive integer _t_, let \[_t_\]={0_,...,t_-1}.

### 3.1 The external-memory model and sorting bound

Let _N,M,B,w_ be positive integers with \(N\ge 2\). The input consists of _N_ integers of _w_ bits stored on disk, where \(w=\Theta(logN)\). A storage unit of _w_ bits is called a _machine word_, and each input integer occupies one word. The algorithm must write the integers back to disk in nondecreasing order.

Memory holds _M_ words, each disk block contains _B_ consecutive words, and \(2B\le M\le N\). A _block transfer_ reads one disk block into memory or writes one block from memory to disk. The algorithm may access any disk block, and its complexity is the total number of block transfers.

Disk data must be read into memory before they can participate in computation; computation in memory is not charged as I/O. The algorithm may perform arbitrary bit operations on integers, including combining bits from different integers into intermediate results. Data buffers and mutable workspace count toward the _M_-word memory bound.

The program is fixed from the size parameters, independently of the input values, and its code is excluded from data space. When \(w<\lceil log_2N\rceil\) and _M_ is below a fixed threshold, the construction stores its predetermined execution-step index outside the _M_ words. The threshold depends only on the construction and the constants in \(w=\Theta(logN)\). The step index specifies the position in a sequence fixed before the input values are known; it is not a buffer for input data. Appendix D gives the detailed conventions and formalization scope.

The input, output, and intermediate data on disk together occupy at most _O(N<sup>k</sup>_) words for a constant _k_ independent of _N,M,B_. We call this _polynomial disk space_. Disk addresses therefore occupy _O_(log_N_) bits, or a constant number of machine words.

**Theorem 3.1** (External-memory integer sorting)**.** Under these conventions, there is a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(2B\le M\le N\), _N_ integers of \(\Theta(logN)\) bits can be sorted deterministically in

\(O\big(\frac{N}{B}\big[1+\frac{logN}{(log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(logM)^\varepsilon}\big]\big)\) (2)

block transfers. The algorithm uses at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space, and is correct on every input.

Here \(\varepsilon\) is independent of _N,M,B_; we take \(\varepsilon=1.5\times 10^{-5}\). The factor _N/B_ is the cost of scanning the input. The logarithmic factor in classical sorting is governed mainly by the number of blocks that fit in memory. Our bound depends on both log(_M/B_) and log_M_, reducing the cost when memory holds only a small number of blocks.

1 gives two examples with _M_=2_B_, both with saving factor \((logB)^\varepsilon\).

When the input fits in memory, reading, sorting, and writing it takes the optimal _O(N/B_) block transfers.

## 3.2 The communication model and coding counterexample

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a finite undirected network. An edge _e_ has capacity _c(e_), shared by the two directions: their transmission rates must sum to at most _c(e_). The network has _W_ unicast sessions. Session _i_ has source _s<sub>i</sub>_, sink \(t_i\neq s_i\), and required rate _r<sub>i</sub>_. Source _s<sub>i</sub>_ holds a message _X<sub>i</sub>_<tbc>

Under _fractional routing_, each session may use several source-sink paths. Assign nonnegative flow to the paths of session _i_ so that their sum is _r<sub>i</sub>_. For every edge, the total flow on all paths using it must not exceed its capacity; this sum includes both directions and all sessions.

_Network coding_ allows nodes to transmit functions of their source messages and previously received information. Each sink must recover its required message for every source input, giving a zero-error requirement. For fixed network, capacities, and source-sink pairs, the simultaneously achievable rate vectors and their limits form the corresponding _capacity region_. The multiple- unicast conjecture asserts that the coding and fractional routing capacity regions coincide. A rate vector achievable by coding but not by routing therefore refutes it.

All edges in our counterexample have unit capacity. We use a finite-round binary linear protocol: every transmitted bit is an exclusive-or (XOR), or sum modulo two, of bits already available at the transmitting node, and transmission times and directions are fixed in advance. In each round, each edge carries at most one bit in one direction, computed only from initial messages or information received in earlier rounds. Local computation and storage are unrestricted. If a protocol delivers _k_ bits from each source to its sink in _T_ rounds, its _common rate_ is _k/T_. Let _R_route be the maximum common rate under fractional routing, and let _R_code be the supremum of common rates achievable by these binary linear protocols.

The finite construction used in this paper also yields the following communication result.

**Theorem 3.2** (A strict coding advantage in undirected networks)**.** There is a finite undirected network with unit edge capacities and independent source messages such that

\(R_\text{route}\le 1-\frac{33}{338432}<1=R_\text{code}.\) (3)

A finite binary linear block code achieves a common rate strictly above this routing upper bound. The network can also be chosen to be a simple graph, with no loops or parallel edges.

## 4 Proof Overview

The central idea is to use a coding circuit for data rearrangement. The same circuit can deliver independent messages to their destinations and break a large array-movement task into subtasks that each handle less data. We first explain the movement needed for sorting, then show why a coding counterexample provides an implementation using fewer block transfers.

### 4.1 Rearrangement in sorting

Arrange the input integers in a table, storing each column contiguously on disk. Sorting every column does not necessarily remove inversions between columns. Classical Columnsort alternates sorting columns with prescribed rearrangements that redistribute the data among new columns. These movements bring integers from different original columns together for comparison. Executing the column sorts and movements in the prescribed order produces a sorted sequence.

A _rearrangement_ moves data from their original positions to other positions while preserving every value. Figure 1 illustrates a row-column interchange: each destination is determined by the original row and column indices, independently of the data values. The new columns contain<tbc>

<tbc>integers from different original columns, allowing subsequent column sorts to compare previously separated values.

We accelerate these movements determined by position. The algorithm may form linear combinations of integer bits along the way, but ultimately restores the input integer that belongs at each destination. The rearrangements required by Columnsort have a special structure: they can be expressed using a constant number of exchanges of two fields in an address, together with sequential scans, which read or write an array in its storage order.

## 4.2 Circuits and the coding counterexample

A coding counterexample requires both a scheme recovering every message and a proof that routing on the same network cannot achieve its rate. A finite circuit specifies a predetermined sequence of XOR operations. Bits may be mixed in intermediate steps, but each original bit must reach its designated output. Turning the circuit wires into network edges gives a coding scheme; assigning matrix labels to nodes will bound the routing rate.

## 4.3 Using coding to accelerate address interchange

An array element’s _address_ is its position numbered from zero; a consecutive group of digits in its representation is a _field_. Exchanging two fields specifies each element’s new position while keeping the other fields fixed. In Figure 3, the element at position 28 moves to position 42. If its original value is 7, it remains 7 after the move: rearrangement changes positions and preserves values.

Let _H,D_ be the fields to exchange. Split each into _m_ equal short fields and regard the short fields as the coordinates of two vectors. An orthogonal projection _P_ keeps the component in a chosen subspace and removes its perpendicular component; write _I_ for the identity matrix. We call the following address operation a _partial swap_:

\((H,D)\longmapsto\big((I-P)H+PD,PH+(I-P)D\big).\)

It exchanges the components in the image of _P_ and keeps the complementary components fixed. Projection zero does nothing, and projection _I_ exchanges the whole fields. Address arithmetic uses a suitable fixed radix; the stored data remain bits, and all circuit gates still use XOR.

Fixing the address digits before _H_ selects a contiguous _prefix segment_. Distribute these equal- length segments cyclically among the circuit’s _W_ inputs. Each input now holds a _stream_, an ordered sequence of bits on disk, containing 1_/W_ of the original array. A gate’s subspace specifies the same storage order for every incident stream, so XOR of corresponding positions still implements the original gate. For nested subspaces, the rank of the difference of their projection matrices equals the difference of their dimensions. Temporary copies undergo the same changes of storage order and their costs are included.

The XOR circuit ultimately returns every bit to the correct output stream. The source and sink partial swaps compose to the full interchange, so each recovered bit also has its correct new address. Restoring the original segment order removes the circuit’s permutation of streams. Thus the new construction performs the full field interchange directly.

When the projection _P_ has rank _r_, the partial swap decomposes into _r_ operations, each exchanging a one-dimensional component. Each such operation first changes coordinates by a lower- triangular matrix, exchanges one pair of short fields, and undoes the coordinate change. The two coordinate changes use scans, leaving exactly _r_ recursive exchanges. Section 6 gives the matrices and proves the memory bound.

The total is _S_ child exchanges, each on _V/W_ bits and fields 1_/m_ as wide. Ordinary pairwise exchange would use _m_ children on the whole array. ### 4.4 From rearrangement to sorting

For an array of at most _M_<sup>2</sup> integers, use the Columnsort procedure introduced above. Column sorts recursively handle shorter columns until they fit in memory, while fixed intercolumn rearrangements invoke the coded address interchange. A suitable table shape gives constant recursion depth. Section 7 proves correctness and the local sorting bound

\(O\left(1+\frac{n}{B}\left[1+\left(\frac{logM}{log(M/B)}\right)^{1-\varepsilon}\right]\right),n\le M^2.\)

For larger inputs, use most-significant-digit radix sorting: partition by the highest bit group, then process the next bit group within each bucket. High-order bits already determine the order between buckets. Once a bucket is small enough, sort it with the local algorithm. If every bit group has been processed, all its integers are equal and recursion can also stop.

One partition first divides the input into subarrays of size \(\Theta(M^2)\) and sorts each by the current bit group. Each group value then occupies at most one contiguous interval per subarray. Store the start and length of each interval, then concatenate intervals having the same bit-group value to form a bucket. Choosing \(\Theta(logM)\) bits per round keeps the number of intervals small enough that concatenation and boundary handling cost only a scan.

Buckets at the same recursion depth are disjoint and contain at most _N_ integers altogether. The local sorting bound controls each level’s cost. Since each integer has \(\Theta(logN)\) bits, there are _O_(log_N/_log_M_) levels. Combining these bounds yields

\(O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{logN}{(log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(logM)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)\)

block transfers. For \(N\le M^2\), the local bound also implies this bound. Section 8 supplies the partition and recursion analysis and combines it with direct sorting for bounded memory parameters to complete the main proof.

## 5 A Counterexample to the Multiple-Unicast Conjecture

This section proves Theorem 3.2. We first construct a linear circuit that exchanges two collections of inputs and interpret its connections as an undirected communication network. We then assign matrix labels to the network to show that every routing scheme has a common rate strictly below an achievable coding rate. The same matrix relations will accelerate address interchange in the next section. The starting point is an explicit finite list of XOR operations, together with subspace labels used to analyze it. We combine copies of this circuit so that auxiliary registers can be reused. The labels then specify how arrays are reordered during the I/O algorithm. The next subsections give the finite circuit, explain how its copies are combined, and derive the routing bound; Section 6 gives the address permutations.

Our circuits consist of registers and XOR gates. Each register stores one bit. A gate reads the current values of specified registers and updates some of them according to a prescribed linear rule; registers not updated retain their values. A gate acting on _r_ registers is thus a linear map \(g:\mathbb{F}_2^r\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_2^r\), where F<sub>2</sub>={0,1} with addition and multiplication modulo two. We specify its action directly by register names: for example, \(y\leftarrow y+x\) replaces _y_ by the XOR of the two current values and leaves _x_ unchanged. The circuit executes its gates in a predetermined order.

In the circuit diagram, each gate is a vertex. For each register, wires connect the gates involving it in execution order, with an input and an output at the two ends of this path. A wire entering a gate carries the value before the update, and the outgoing wire carries the value after it. Thus a register persists along a path of wire segments, and its value may change at a gate. All wires participating in a gate meet at its vertex, which computes the register value for each outgoing wire.

To compare coding with routing, regard every wire segment as an undirected edge of unit capacity, obtaining a graph _G_=(V_,E_). Write _s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>i</sub>_ for the input and output of register path _i_. If the circuit sends all initial values to the outputs according to a permutation \(\sigma\), create the sessions \(s_i\rightarrow t_{\sigma(i)}\) and give the sources independent messages. The gate computations specify how to encode these messages. Routing may use an edge in either direction, with the two directions sharing its capacity; the circuit order specifies only how this particular coding scheme runs. Edges belonging to different register paths are retained separately, so the graph may contain parallel edges.

A temporary wire is created by copying an existing value and ends after its last use. It begins at a copy gate and has no independent source message or session. Such wires are nevertheless edges of the same graph and are included in every capacity and rank sum. Copying and later discarding a value are local linear operations, so they fit the same gate semantics.

## 5.1 A Finite Linear Circuit

We start with a finite circuit on bits and attach subspaces of an eight-dimensional rational vector space to its registers. ## 7 Local Sorting

Address-field interchange rearranges records, but sorting also needs value comparisons. We use classical Columnsort, alternating column sorts with fixed rearrangements that bring records from different columns together for comparison \[Lei85, CC03\]. We first prove Columnsort correct and reduce its rearrangements to address-field interchange, then bound the recursive cost.

A record occupies _O(w_) bits and may be an integer or a constant number of integer fields compared lexicographically. The word size \(w=\Theta(logN)\) is always determined by the global input size _N_. Keep _a_=log(_M/B_) and \(\tau=1-\varepsilon\), and set \(H=\lfloor M/C\rfloor\). Choose the fixed constant _C_ large enough that 512_H_ records, including the two-bit tags used below to distinguish ordinary records from padding, fit in reserved memory, leaving space for buffers and control information. We first assume sufficiently large _M_ and _M/B_; Corollary A.3 transfers the bounds to all \(2B\le M\).

### 7.1 The Columnsort Reduction

Columnsort requires columns long enough to contain the disorder left by its rearrangements. We use _s_ columns of _r=s_<sup>3</sup> records: this shape satisfies the Columnsort conditions and makes column length the 3/4 power of the total size _rs_, allowing recursion to shrink the problem. Taking _s_=2_<sup>t</sup>_ also expresses each record address as four equal-width fields, so the intercolumn rearrangement becomes a rotation of those fields. The next proposition reduces the required movement to six interchanges.

**Proposition 7.1** (The Columnsort reduction)**.** Let _s_=2_<sup>t</sup>_ and _r=s_<sup>3</sup>, where \(t\ge 3\). An array stored as _s_ contiguous columns of _r_ records each can be sorted using four rounds of column sorting, six address-field interchanges of width _t_, and sequential scans. The procedure is correct whenever all column sorts are correct.

_Proof._ Step 2 distributes records from each original column among the new columns for joint sorting; step 4 restores the original column layout. A final half-column shift brings remaining inversions across old boundaries into one column. The eight steps are:

1. Sort each column.<tbc>

2. Move the record at position _j_ to \(\pi(j)=(jmods)r+\lfloor j/s\rfloor\).<tbc>

3. Sort each rearranged column.<tbc>

4. Apply the inverse permutation \(\pi^{-1}\).<tbc>

5. Sort each column.<tbc>

6. Prepend _r/_2 negative sentinels and append _r/_2 positive sentinels, shifting column boundaries by half a column. There are now _s_+1 columns, each still of length _r_.<tbc>

7. Sort these _s_+1 columns.<tbc>

8. Delete the first and last _r/_2 records.

Negative sentinels precede every ordinary record, and positive sentinels follow every ordinary record. A two-bit tag distinguishes the three types. All sentinels of one type use the same canonical record. Recursion reuses the same tag and removes exactly the multiplicity of sentinels introduced by the current call.

The parameters satisfy even _r_, _s|r_, and \(r\ge 2s(s+1)\). First consider zero-one inputs. After step 1, write the number of zeros in original column _c_ as _Z<sub>c</sub>=a<sub>c</sub>s+b<sub>c</sub>_, with \(0\le b_c<s\). Since _s|r_, step 2 sends _a<sub>c</sub>_+**1**_<sub>d\<b<sub>c</sub></sub>_ zeros from this column to new column _d_. Summing over the _s_ original columns, the new zero counts _z<sub>d</sub>_ satisfy \(z_\mathrm{max}-z_\mathrm{min}\le s\).

After step 3, every entry in a row below _z_<sub>min</sub> is zero, and every entry in a row at least _z_<sub>max</sub> is one. The inverse permutation moves position _dr+q_ to _sq+d_, so after step 4 all possible disorder is confined to the half-open interval

\(I=[sz_\mathrm{min},sz_\mathrm{max}),|I|\le s^2\le r/2;\)

all entries before _I_ are zero, and all entries after it are one. Step 5 preserves these outside regions, since sorting within a column preserves its all-zero prefix and all-one suffix. If _I_ is empty or lies in a single old column, the array is now sorted. Otherwise, _I_=[_A,E_) crosses exactly one old column boundary _b=kr_, and \(E-A\le r/2\) gives \(I\subseteq[b-r/2,b+r/2)\). Prepending half a column of negative sentinels in step 6 moves this interval into the single new column [_b,b+r_). Sorting that column in step 7 therefore sorts the entire padded sequence, including the boundary case |_I_|=_r/_2.

For general ordered records, an inversion in the padded output would admit a nondecreasing threshold map taking its two values to 1 followed by 0, with negative and positive sentinels mapped to 0 and 1. This map commutes with fixed rearrangements and with the ordered value sequence produced by each column sort, contradicting the zero-one case. Stability of column sorting is not needed. Every sort and rearrangement preserves the multiset of records. Step 8 removes _r/_2 records from each end of the sorted sequence, exactly cancelling the added sentinel multiplicities. Even if the input already contains sentinels with the same tags, cancellation by multiplicity preserves the original multiset; no recursion-level tags are needed, and no ordinary records are removed. The additional suffix of positive padding is removed by its exact multiplicity in the same way. The output is therefore a sorted permutation of the input.

Since _rs_=2<sup>4_t_</sup>, writing record addresses as four fields of _t_ bits makes \(\pi\) the rotation \([x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]\mapsto[x_4,x_1,x_2,x_3]\). Interchanging fields 3,4, then 2,3, then 1,2 implements \(\pi\); the reverse sequence implements \(\pi^{-1}\). The two permutations therefore need six interchanges in total, and all remaining movement consists of scans. A record’s internal bits move together as an unchanged suffix, without storing a permutation table.

## 7.2 The Local Sorting Bound

Implement column sorts recursively. Since the input has at most the square of memory size, a constant number of reductions in column length suffices to reach an in-memory problem.

**Lemma 7.2** (Local sorting)**.** For \(1\le n\le M^2\), an array of _n_ records can be sorted in

\(O\big(1+\frac{n}{B}[1+(logM/a)^\tau]\big)\) (19)

block transfers, using at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space.

_Proof._ First suppose \(n\le H^2\). For a call on _z_ records, sort in memory if \(z\le 512H\). Otherwise, take \(t=\lceil logz/4\rceil\), _s_=2_<sup>t</sup>_, and _r=s_<sup>3</sup>, pad to _rs_ records with positive sentinels, and apply Proposition 7.1, recursively sorting each column. Remove the new padding after the call, retaining the original _z_ records. Increasing the fixed memory threshold ensures \(s\ge 8\) in every nonterminal call.

After padding, _rs\<_16_z_ and each column has length _r\<_8_z_<sup>3/4</sup>. Each level reduces size to its 3/4 power. Starting from \(n\le H^2\), three levels give column length less than \(128H^{27/32}\le 128H\), below the stopping threshold. The four rounds of column sorting in a call have total input length (4_s_+1)_r=O(z_). Thus the recursion has constant depth and processes _O(n_) records in total, including padding and repeated sorts.

Each interchange acts on _O(zw_) bits with field width _O_(log_M_). Lemma 6.1 bounds its cost by \(O(1+(z/B)[1+(logM/a)^\tau])\). Short columns that fit in memory share sequential input and output streams: read and sort one column at a time, appending the results. A round processing _L_ records costs only _O_(1+_L/B_) transfers. Nonterminal calls have length \(\Omega(M)\), so their scan cost absorbs startup. Summing over the levels proves (19).

For \(H^2<n\le M^2\), sort a constant number of subarrays and perform a constant number of two-way merge rounds, each costing a scan. Execute depth first and reuse memory; each parent retains only a constant number of descriptor words, and temporary disk arrays have polynomial size. Corollary A.3 restores the original parameters. If _M_ is bounded, then \(n\le M^2\) is also bounded and direct comparison sorting suffices.

## 8 Sorting Arbitrary Input Sizes

The local algorithm sorts individual subarrays but does not determine their order relative to one another. We use most-significant-digit radix sorting: partition by the highest bit group, then process the next group within each bucket, sorting a bucket directly once it is small enough for the local algorithm. A _bit group_ is a consecutive group of binary digits, and a _bucket_ contains records sharing the current bit-group value.

Keep \(H=\lfloor M/C\rfloor\) and _a_=log(_M/B_), and write _h_=log_M_. Each bit group has \(t=\lfloor logH\rfloor=\Theta(h)\) bits and at most \(K=2^t\le H\) values; a shorter highest group uses its actual width. We first work with the simulated parameters supplied by Lemma A.2, whose memory-to-block ratio can be made larger than any fixed constant. Increase that ratio threshold _R_<sub>0</sub> so that \(H\ge B\). Corollary A.3 restores the original parameters.

### 8.1 The Cost of One Partition

Processing \(\Theta(logM)\) bits per round may create \(\Theta(M)\) buckets. Reserving one block buffer per bucket would require \(\Theta(MB)\) words and need not fit in memory. Instead, sort each subarray by the current bit group so that each bucket occupies a contiguous interval, then read and concatenate these intervals one at a time. This uses a fixed number of block buffers, at the cost of boundary transfers for each interval. We show that these transfers still fit within scan cost.

**Lemma 8.1** (Partitioning by one bit group)**.** An array of length _n\>H_<sup>2</sup> can be partitioned by a bit group of at most _t_ bits into contiguous buckets in increasing bit-group order, using

\(O\big(\frac{n}{B}[1+(h/a)^\tau]\big)\)

block transfers. After local sorting, interval concatenation alone takes _O(n/B_) transfers.

_Proof._ Divide the current storage order into \(J=\lceil n/H^2\rceil\) contiguous subarrays, each with at most _H_<sup>2</sup> records. Apply Lemma 7.2 to sort each subarray by the current bit group. Since _J=O(n/H_<sup>2</sup>), the total sorting cost satisfies the stated bound.

After sorting, each value occupies at most one contiguous interval in a subarray. Scan the subarrays and store each interval’s start and length in an auxiliary array on disk, indexed by subarray number and bit-group value. Each entry occupies a constant number of words, and empty intervals have length zero. Read the corresponding intervals in increasing bit-group order, appending complete records to the output stream to form contiguous buckets.

The auxiliary array has _JK=O(n/H_) entries. Each entry access and interval boundary costs a constant number of transfers, while every record is copied exactly once. Concatenation therefore costs _O(n/B+n/H_)=_O(n/B_) transfers and uses a fixed number of block buffers. The buckets are ordered by the current bit group; later bit groups and local sorting determine the order within each bucket.

## 8.2 The Cost of High-Order Recursion

After partitioning, high-order bits determine the order between buckets, and the remaining work takes place within buckets. Put _p_=log(_N/M_).

**Proposition 8.2** (Sorting large inputs)**.** For \(N\ge M^2\), the _N_ input integers can be sorted in

\(O\big(\frac{N}{B}\big[1+\frac{p}{a^\tau h^\varepsilon}\big]\big)\)

block transfers, using at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space.

_Proof._ All integers in a subproblem share the high-order bits already processed. If its length is at most _H_<sup>2</sup>, use Lemma 7.2 to sort by the complete integers. If no bit groups remain, all integers are equal and can be output directly. Otherwise, apply Lemma 8.1 and recursively process the nonempty buckets in increasing bucket order, advancing to the next bit group. High-order bits order the buckets, and recursion sorts each bucket, proving correctness.

Subproblems at one depth are disjoint and contain at most _N_ records in total. Those requiring further partitioning have length greater than _H_<sup>2</sup> and produce _O(N/H_<sup>2</sup>) subarrays altogether. Lemma 8.1 gives the per-level cost

\(O\big(\frac{N}{B}[1+(h/a)^\tau]\big).\) (20)

There are _O(N/H_) auxiliary entries, new buckets, and tasks at that depth. Newly formed short buckets have total length at most _N_; Lemma 7.2 bounds their sorting, startup, and final output by (20) as well. Long buckets with no remaining bit groups require only a scan to output.

Each level processes \(\Theta(h)\) bits, and integer width is _O_(log_N_), so the depth is _O_(log_N/h_). For \(N\ge M^2\), we have \(p\ge h\) and \(logN\le 2p\). Multiplying the per-level cost by the depth and using \(a\le h\) proves the claimed bound.

Execute depth first, storing each pending bucket’s start, length, and bit-group position on a disk task stack in a constant number of words. Append sorted buckets to the final output stream. Memory holds only the active task and buffers. The recursion depth is _O_(log_N_), and temporary disk space is polynomial. Finally apply Corollary A.3.

## 8.3 An Alternative Using Individual Record Accesses

The following algorithm does not use the coding construction. We use it when _M_ is below the fixed memory threshold.

**Lemma 8.3** (A linear number of individual record accesses)**.** For every \(M\ge 2B\), an array of _N_ integers of \(w=\Theta(logN)\) bits can be sorted in _O(N_) block transfers, using at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space.

_Proof._ Use least-significant-digit radix sorting: process bit groups from the lowest to the highest, preserving the order of records with equal current-group values in each pass. On disk, handle \(\lfloor logN\rfloor\) bits per pass, so only a constant number of passes is needed. A pass initializes \(\Theta(N)\) counters, counts bit-group values record by record, and scans the counters to compute bucket starting positions. It then reads records in input order, writes each to the next free position of its bucket, and updates that position pointer. Equal values are written in read order, preserving the order established by earlier low-order groups. Each record accesses a constant number of disk locations, for _O(N_) transfers per pass.

Random writes use read-modify-write with one physical block buffer; the remaining memory holds the current record and control state. If _M_ is a bounded number of words, storing a constant number of state words on disk adds only a constant number of transfers per record. The counters, temporary arrays, and addresses satisfy the required space bounds.

## 8.4 Proof of the Main Sorting Theorem

Combining the preceding algorithms according to input size proves Theorem 3.1.

_Proof of Theorem 3.1._ Keep _a_=log(_M/B_), _h_=log_M_, _p_=log(_N/M_), and \(\tau=1-\varepsilon\). If the input fits in memory, reading, sorting, and writing it takes _O(N/B_) block transfers. For \(M\le N\le M^2\), Lemma 7.2 gives local sorting. Its constant startup cost is absorbed by \(N/B\ge 2\), and \(logN\ge h\) gives

\(1+(h/a)^\tau=1+\frac{h}{a^\tau h^\varepsilon}\le 1+\frac{logN}{a^\tau h^\varepsilon}.\)

For \(N\ge M^2\), Proposition 8.2 gives cost factor \(1+p/(a^\tau h^\varepsilon)\), which also satisfies (2) because \(p\le logN\).

All these algorithms are deterministic, correct on every input, and satisfy the memory and polynomial disk-space requirements. Corollary A.3 covers every memory-to-block-size ratio. If _M_ is below the fixed threshold, then _B_ is bounded, and the _O(N_) cost in Lemma 8.3 is also _O(N/B_). Taking the fixed constant \(\varepsilon=1.5\times 10^{-5}>0\) proves the theorem.

## 9 Conclusion

We turn the communication savings of a finite linear circuit into recursive address-field interchange and combine it with Columnsort and most-significant-digit radix sorting to obtain a deterministic external-memory integer sorting algorithm. Its I/O upper bound asymptotically improves on classical comparison sorting in some parameter ranges. The same finite construction also gives a strict coding advantage in an undirected multiple-unicast network.

Directions for further work include improving the finite coding construction to increase the saving exponent and developing simpler, more efficient algorithmic implementations. It is also natural to ask whether network coding can accelerate other data-movement tasks in a similar way.

## A Buffered I/O and Memory Simulation

### A.1 Simulating sequential tape access

Put _b=Bw_, the number of bits in a disk block. A tape here is a packed bit sequence with one head; an elementary step reads or changes the bit under the head and moves it by at most one position. A fixed alphabet and a fixed number of tracks change the packing density only by a constant factor. This definition does not permit arbitrary jumps to data elsewhere on a tape.

**Lemma A.1** (Buffered tape phases)**.** Fix the number of tapes. A phase of _T_ elementary tape steps, including all head movements, can be simulated with _O(B_) resident words and _O_(1+_T/(Bw_)) block transfers. For _J_ separately activated phases, with total step count _T_, the bound is _O(J+T/(Bw_)), including writing modified (dirty) buffers back to disk.

_Proof._ For each tape, keep the block containing its head and its two neighbors. At activation, load this three-block window, with the current block in the middle. While the head stays in the window, its operations incur no transfers. Upon exit, write back the dirty blocks and load a new window centered on the new current block. The head must move at least _b_ positions between two such exits: it starts somewhere in the middle block and must cross a whole neighboring block before leaving the window. Each replacement uses at most a constant number of transfers. Thus a tape with _T<sub>i</sub>_ head movements costs _O_(1+_T<sub>i</sub>/b_) transfers, including the initial load and final writeback. Summing over the fixed number of tapes proves the first bound. Apply it separately to the _J_ phases for the second. Reversing direction does not invalidate a window, so short alternating accesses to adjacent blocks do not introduce a transfer per tape step.

The stream transformations in Section 6 satisfy the lemma’s hypothesis. In particular, the controlled-shift and scaling procedures of OpenAI [Ope26, Lemmas 3-4] concatenate the work streams for successive fixed-prefix segments; a new segment does not start a new buffer allocation. Their local reversals, head returns, and erasures are included in the linear tape-step bound. Within one recursion node there are only a fixed number of such elementary procedures. Arithmetic on call descriptors uses a fixed number of machine words of width _w_ and free resident computation in our I/O model. Its operands are dimensions, offsets, and addresses bounded by a fixed polynomial in _N_.

## A.2 Suspending and restoring recursive calls

OpenAI \[Ope26, Proposition 11, fixed-tape depth-first schedule\] explicitly parks inactive streams and restores them between child calls, charging this movement to the parent. Random disk access permits the following variant, in which inactive streams stay in place. This also specifies the transfer costs at call boundaries, which are not covered by the amortization within a single tape phase.

Each active call has a fixed number of disk regions: one for each stream assigned to a circuit register, together with temporary work tapes. Each region is packed and block-aligned, with its length and head position in the call descriptor. Regions belonging to different suspended calls are disjoint. The child reads one designated register stream of its parent as input; the child’s own register streams and work regions are allocated separately. Fresh work regions are initialized by scans within the _O(V_) local work budget. Only the active call owns the tape windows. Suspended calls have no resident buffers.

Before descending, finish the current local procedure, flush all dirty windows, and write a stack frame containing the parent dimensions, region addresses, head positions, the instruction to resume, and the child index. Adjacent irrelevant coordinates are collapsed, so this frame has a fixed number of machine words, independent of recursion depth. A frame occupies a fixed number of block-aligned disk blocks at the stack top; writing or reading it costs _O_(1) transfers even when _B_=1. The child then reuses the same window buffers and control workspace. All inactive parent streams remain on disk and are not traversed.

On return, write back the child’s windows and place its output in the designated parent register stream, using a scan of _V/W_ bits if a copy is needed. Read and remove the top stack frame, restore the parent’s descriptor, and reload its windows as needed. The child’s temporary regions can then be reused. No restoration scans an ancestor’s data or searches past another stack frame. Output copying costs _O_(1+_V/(WBw_)) per child; flushing, stack access, and window reactivation cost _O_(1) per child. The fixed number _S_ of children therefore adds _O_(1+_V/(Bw_)) transfers per parent node, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed circuit. It does not change the recursive volume multiplier _S/W_.

Together with Lemma A.1, this yields the node recurrence in Lemma 6.2. It also accounts for the constant overhead when a child reaches the stopping condition set by the available memory. The active windows, one stack-transfer buffer, and the descriptor occupy _c_<sub>1</sub>_B+c_<sub>2</sub> words for fixed constants _c_<sub>1</sub>_,c_<sub>2</sub>; the normalization below reserves this space. Ancestor regions and frames use polynomial disk space: a depth-first execution has depth _O_(log(2+_e_)), finitely many regions per level, and no level has volume larger than the padded root volume. All stored addresses therefore fit in a fixed number of machine words of width _w_.

The simulations, subarray sorts, and merges preserve correctness, the _M_-word memory bound, and polynomial disk space.

We first take a few high-order digits from the fields being interchanged, using existing data to create enough segments, then pad their count to the required multiple. Once the count is sufficiently large, padding costs only a constant factor in volume. We decompose the remaining width into recursive scales and interchange the corresponding pairs. Keep the parameters of that section, with \(t_0=\Theta(log(M/B))\).

### Removing padding before restoration.

After all complete chunk swaps, scan the layout (_p,s,D_<sub>-</sub>_,g,H_<sub>-</sub>_,z_) and discard exactly those segments with \(s\ge R\). Every complete chunk swap fixes (_p,s_) and is a bit-value-preserving permutation, so no valid bit enters a discarded segment; those segments remain zero. Intermediate coded states need not satisfy this property, which is why removal occurs only after the complete swaps. Concatenate the retained segments, decode _s_ as (_D_<sub>+</sub>_,H_<sub>+</sub>), and then apply _F_ in (22). The widths, padding tests, and chunk descriptions depend only on the dimensions and are generated using a fixed number of counters, each occupying a constant number of machine words of width _w_. All scans share their stream buffers across prefixes; recursive calls and chunk swaps run sequentially and reuse workspace. ## D Formal Verification

We use Lean 4 and Mathlib [dUU21,The20] to formally verify the correctness and complexity bounds of the external-memory integer sorting algorithm in Theorem 3.1, with \(\varepsilon=3/200000=1.5\times 10^{-5}\). The verification covers the full parameter range \(2B\le M\le N\): for every input, the algorithm terminates, outputs the integers in nondecreasing order with their multiplicities preserved, uses at most _M_ words of memory and polynomial disk space, and satisfies the stated I/O bound. These guarantees include the input/output format conversions.

The formalization uses the external-memory model of Section 3. One I/O reads or writes a block of _B_ words. Computation uses only data already read into memory, and data buffers and mutable workspace count toward the _M_-word limit. The program is fixed from the size parameters before the input is given, and in-memory computation is not charged as I/O. Storage of program code and the predetermined execution-step index follows the conventions in that section.
